$comment: Shared behavioural contract for the dictionary correction pass.
The macOS app (Swift) and the Windows app (C#) implement this logic independently.
Independent implementations drift. This file is the thing that stops them: both must
run every case below and produce exactly the stated output. A change to correction
semantics starts here, not in either implementation.
1. Whole matches only  - a rule must never bite into a longer word.
2. Case-insensitive    - the trigger matches in any case; output is verbatim.
3. Longest match first - a longer trigger wins over a shorter overlapping one.
4. Glued words match   - parts may be separated by any number of spaces or hyphens,
5. Disabled is inert   - a disabled entry changes nothing.
6. Diacritics fold     - matching ignores accents in both directions, so a trigger
of 'nunez' matches 'Nuñez' and a trigger of 'nuñez'
matches 'Nunez'. The replacement is inserted verbatim.
7. NFC throughout      - trigger, text and replacement are all composed before
matching, whether or not the dictionary holds any rules.

cases.name: basic phrase replacement
cases.input: I use cloud code every day.
cases.expected: I use Claude Code every day.

cases.name: glued together with no separator
cases.expected: I use Claude Code every day.

cases.name: joined by a hyphen
cases.expected: I use Claude Code every day.

cases.name: multiple spaces between parts
cases.input: I use cloud  code every day.
cases.expected: I use Claude Code every day.

cases.name: trigger matches regardless of case
must not corrupt a longer word that starts the same way
must not touch the ordinary word alone
cases.input: The cloud is fine and the code is fine.
cases.expected: The cloud is fine and the code is fine.

cases.name: longest trigger wins over a shorter overlapping one
counts repeated hits
cases.input: clawed code, then clawed code again, and clawed code.
cases.expected: Claude Code, then Claude Code again, and Claude Code.

cases.name: punctuation is a boundary
a possessive still matches - the apostrophe is not a letter
a disabled entry changes nothing
cases.input: I use cloud code every day.
cases.expected: I use cloud code every day.

cases.name: a term entry never rewrites text
single word trigger is honoured when asked for
several independent rules in one pass
empty input is left alone
replacement containing regex metacharacters is literal
trigger containing regex metacharacters is literal
accented trigger matches decomposed input (NFC normalization)
cases.$comment: macOS hands back NFD strings from several APIs. Without normalizing both sides, an accented trigger silently never fires. Input here is deliberately NFD.

cases.name: an unaccented trigger matches accented text
cases.$comment: The dominant case for a Spanish speaker, not an edge case: the engine writes “Andújar” while the user's rule says “andujar”. Matching folds diacritics; the replacement is still inserted exactly as the user wrote it.

cases.name: an accented trigger matches unaccented text
cases.$comment: The mirror of the case above. Folding has to be symmetric, or the user is back to hand-enumerating variants from the other end.

cases.name: ñ and n are interchangeable in both directions
cases.$comment: All four spellings of the name are one trigger. “nunez” is the rule; the three accented spellings in the input are what the engine actually produces.

cases.name: an uppercase accented word is matched
cases.$comment: Case folding and diacritic folding have to compose. Both cases of every accented letter are listed in the pattern rather than left to the engine's own folding, because .NET and ICU do not fold identically.

cases.name: inverted Spanish punctuation is a boundary, not part of the word
cases.$comment: ¿ and ¡ are punctuation, so the fence opens and closes around them exactly as it does for an ordinary question mark.

cases.name: the word fence still holds once diacritics are folded
cases.$comment: Widening the pattern must not widen the fence. A folded trigger is still a whole match or no match at all.
cases.input: un caso anodino y un piano
cases.expected: un caso anodino y un piano

cases.name: folding diacritics is symmetric, and the cost is accepted
cases.$comment: The trade, written down rather than left to be discovered: a rule for “ano” also fires on “año”. Accent-blind matching cannot tell them apart. For a dictionary of names and technical terms that is the right side of the trade, and pinning it here keeps it a decision.
cases.input: hace un ano y otro año
cases.expected: hace un año y otro año

cases.name: an empty rule set still normalizes to NFC
cases.$comment: Normalization must not depend on whether the user happens to own any correction rules. A default install has an empty dictionary and still has to emit composed text. Input here is deliberately NFD.

cases.name: a combining mark is part of the word, not a boundary
cases.$comment: NFC leaves a mark standing wherever no precomposed form exists - there is no q-with-acute - so marks do reach the matcher. Treating one as a boundary would let a rule bite the base letters off the front of a word, so the fence covers marks as well as letters and digits. Input here is deliberately decomposed.
